issues.legal_issue: A court-sale purchaser seeking delivery of property occupied by tenants or other persons entitled to occupy it is entitled to symbolic rather than actual physical possession when the occupants do not fall within the categories permitting physical delivery.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the property at a court auction and applied for possession under Order XXI Rules 95 and 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The occupants held different portions as tenants of the former owner and were not the judgment-debtors or persons occupying on their behalf.
The occupants did not claim under a title created by the judgment-debtor after attachment; there had been no attachment in the case.
The purchaser was an outsider to the mortgage suit and was not the mortgagee.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled only to symbolic possession of the portions occupied by the tenants, not actual physical possession. The order directing physical possession was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure, actual physical possession may be delivered when the property is occupied by the judgment-debtor, someone on the judgment-debtor’s behalf, or someone claiming under a title created by the judgment-debtor after attachment. Under Rule 96, symbolic possession is delivered when the property is occupied by a tenant or another person entitled to occupy it. The purchaser’s mode of obtaining possession after the sale becomes absolute is governed by these rules. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act concerns dealings by parties to the pending suit or proceeding; the Court did not decide the validity of the tenancies or the application of Sections 52 and 65A to them. M/s Supreme General Films Exchange Ltd. v. His Highness Maharaja Sir Brijnath Singhji Deo concerned a mortgagee’s declaratory suit, and Mangru Mahto v. Shri Thakur Taraknath Tarakeshwar Math concerned a suit for possession by a mortgagee-purchaser, so neither decided an outsider purchaser’s application under Rules 95 and 96. Jayaram Mudaliar v. Ayya Swami was considered in explaining the scope of Section 52.

predicates.court_sale_possession_application: A purchaser at a court sale applied to the court for delivery of the purchased property.
predicates.outsider_auction_purchaser: The person seeking delivery purchased the property at auction and was not a party to the suit that led to the sale.
predicates.occupants_are_tenants_or_other_entitled_: The property was occupied by tenants or other persons entitled to occupy it.
predicates.occupants_outside_debtor_related_categor: The occupants were not the judgment-debtors, were not occupying on their behalf, and were not claiming under a title created by the judgment-debtors after attachment.

issues.definition: When an outsider who purchased property at a court sale applies for delivery and the property is occupied by tenants or other entitled occupants outside the debtor-related categories, the purchaser receives symbolic possession only.
